Step Functions orchestrates serverless workflows with visual execution graphs, per-state retries/catches, and integrations to Lambda, Glue, and more. Pipeline-native monitoring (Airflow SLAs, Step Functions/CloudWatch alarms on task duration) watches every task against the deadline and alerts early.
Event-driven triggers (S3 Event Notifications, EventBridge) start pipelines on arrival with low latency, and idempotent tasks make duplicate events safe.

Failure handling: manual Lambda chaining reinvents error handling; one giant Lambda couples everything; bash on EC2 is fragile. Blind infinite retries are the current failure; ignoring/deleting loses data.

example.code:
Pipeline: 50 tasks, dependencies,
retries, SLAs. Team knows Airflow.
Need: managed service.
example.walkthrough: MWAA provides managed Apache Airflow — DAGs with dependencies, retries, and SLA monitoring without managing the orchestrator. Single-EC2 cron is a single point of failure; manual runs don't scale; Lambda alone lacks DAG orchestration semantics.

pitfalls: Common trap: event-driven triggers (S3 events, EventBridge) + idempotent tasks.
Common trap: separate dev/staging/prod with promotion of tested artifacts.
Common trap: lambda alone for 50-step DAGs.
Common trap: one pipeline for dev and prod.

lessons.title: Analytics — Core concepts
concepts: QuickSight: row-level (and column-level) security in QuickSight and Lake Formation filters data by viewer identity — enforced, not advisory. QuickSight provides managed BI with SPICE in-memory engine, integrating natively with AWS data sources and scaling to hundreds of users.
BI: one-off queries repeat the waste; bigger warehouses just scan faster at higher cost; BI-only caching is fragile. Custom builds reintroduce ops; email chains and screenshots aren't BI.
ML for analysts: redshift ML and SageMaker Canvas let analysts build and use models with SQL or no-code interfaces against warehouse data in place.
Open table formats (Apache Hudi, Iceberg — supported by Athena, EMR, Glue) bring upserts, deletes, and time travel to S3 data lakes.
Materialized views or scheduled aggregation tables precompute the repeated aggregations once, so dashboards read megabytes instead of terabytes.

example.code:
Requirement: managers see only
their region's data in dashboards.

lessons.title: AWS Data Analytics — Core concepts
concepts: Design around the analytics flow: ingest (Kinesis for streaming, batch loads for scheduled), store (S3 data lake in open formats), catalog (Glue Data Catalog as the shared metadata layer), process (Glue/EMR), and consume (Athena for ad-hoc, Redshift for heavy BI, QuickSight for dashboards).

The data lake's economics live in file layout: partition by time or key, store as Parquet/ORC with compression, and avoid the small-files problem. These choices decide whether Athena queries cost cents or dollars.

Streaming systems scale on keys and shards: Kinesis throughput is per-shard, so high-cardinality partition keys and right-sized shard counts are the design levers; Firehose fits delivery-to-destination streaming without consumer management.

Choose the query engine by pattern: Athena for serverless ad-hoc SQL on S3, Redshift (provisioned or Serverless) for complex joins at warehouse scale, EMR for Spark-scale transformations and ML preprocessing. One engine rarely serves all three well.

Build pipelines that heal: Glue job bookmarks for idempotent retries, dead-letter routing for malformed records, schema evolution in the catalog, and alerts on repeated failure rather than on every hiccup.

example.code:
aws athena start-query-execution \
  --query-string "SELECT event_type, count(*) FROM clicks WHERE year='2026' AND month='10' GROUP BY 1" \
  --query-execution-context Database=weblogs --result-configuration OutputLocation=s3://results-bucket/athena/
example.walkthrough: A serverless SQL query against partitioned S3 data — no cluster involved. The WHERE clause on partition columns (year, month) is what keeps Athena from scanning the whole dataset, which is the difference between a cheap query and an expensive one.

pitfalls: Common trap: querying unpartitioned CSV in Athena and paying to scan terabytes for a megabyte answer — partition and use Parquet.
Common trap: low-cardinality Kinesis partition keys — one hot shard throttles the whole stream regardless of shard count.
Common trap: treating the data lake as a file dump with no catalog — undocumented data is undead data; crawl it into the Glue Data Catalog.
Common trap: no job bookmarks on Glue ETL — every retry reprocesses everything and duplicates output.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Aws Data move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Kinesis: Real-Time Streaming
concepts: Data Streams: shards (1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out each), 24h-365d retention, consumers via KCL/Enhanced fan-out; reshard to scale.
Firehose: fully managed delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch — no shard math, near-real-time, with Lambda transforms and format conversion.
Data Analytics (Flink): SQL/streaming analytics on streams; Video Streams for camera feeds with ML integration.
Ordering per shard key; replay by trimming to sequence numbers — the exam's 'reprocess yesterday's events' answer.

example.code:
aws kinesis create-stream --stream-name clicks --shard-count 4
aws kinesis put-record --stream-name clicks --partition-key user123 \
  --data $(echo '{"page":"/home"}' | base64)
example.walkthrough: Partition key spreads load across shards. Need S3 delivery without managing consumers? Firehose. Need replay + multiple apps? Data Streams.

pitfalls: Under-sharding and throttling writes — monitor WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded and reshard.
Using Data Streams when Firehose delivery-to-S3 would do — unnecessary operational load.
Forgetting retention is time-based — extend to 365 days if replay windows are long.
lessons.try_it: Stream records, then use Firehose to land them in S3 as Parquet.

lessons.title: Lambda: Serverless Functions Done Right
concepts: Lambda runs code without servers: you pay per request + GB-second, it scales to thousands of concurrent executions, max 15-minute runtime.
Cold starts hurt latency-sensitive paths — fix with Provisioned Concurrency; keep deployment packages small and reuse execution contexts (init outside the handler).
Event source mappings (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams) poll and invoke synchronously with batching; direct async invokes go to the internal queue with retries and DLQs.
Lambda in a VPC needs ENIs and NAT for internet access — no internet without NAT Gateway (or VPC endpoints for AWS services).

example.walkthrough: Clients created outside the handler survive warm starts. Exam questions about 'reduce cold start impact' want provisioned concurrency + slim packages + init reuse.

pitfalls: Running 20-minute ETL in Lambda — 15-minute max means Step Functions or Fargate instead.
Forgetting VPC Lambdas need NAT for internet — 'Lambda cannot reach the internet' is always the missing NAT route.
Recursive S3→Lambda→S3 loops without idempotency — infinite invocations and a shocking bill.
lessons.try_it: Deploy a function triggered by S3 uploads that logs object keys; check CloudWatch Logs.

lessons.title: EventBridge: Event-Driven Architecture
concepts: EventBridge routes events: AWS services → rules → targets (Lambda, Step Functions, SQS...). The default bus gets all AWS events free.
Custom buses for app events, partner buses for SaaS (Datadog, PagerDuty), schema registry + discovery for typed events.
Rules match event patterns; input transformers reshape payloads; archives + replay reprocess history — unique to EventBridge vs SNS.
Scheduler replaces many cron needs: one-time/future and recurring schedules at scale without managing anything.

example.code:
aws events put-rule --name ec2-state --event-pattern '{
 "source":["aws.ec2"],"detail-type":["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],
 "detail":{"state":["terminated"]}}'
aws events put-targets --rule ec2-state --targets '[{"Id":"1","Arn":"arn:aws:lambda:...:fn:cleanup"}]'
example.walkthrough: Any EC2 termination → cleanup Lambda, automatically. 'React to AWS events' → EventBridge rule + target. Archive/replay is the differentiator over SNS.

pitfalls: Using SNS when you need content-based routing to many targets — EventBridge rules are richer.
Forgetting the default bus already receives AWS service events — no setup needed to start matching.
No archive configured before an incident — replay only works if archiving was on.
lessons.try_it: Route GuardDuty findings to a Lambda via EventBridge and trigger a sample finding.

lessons.title: DynamoDB: Serverless NoSQL at Scale
concepts: Key-value/document store: partition key (+ optional sort key) determines placement; single-digit-ms at any scale; on-demand or provisioned capacity.
GSIs (different partition/sort keys, eventually consistent) vs LSIs (same partition key, 10GB limit, strongly consistent option).
DynamoDB Streams + Lambda = change-data-capture; TTL auto-deletes expired items free; DAX adds microsecond caching; Global Tables = multi-region active-active.
Design by access patterns: model GSIs for your queries, avoid scans, use sparse indexes and composite keys.

example.walkthrough: Composite keys (pk=user, sk=order) let one table serve many access patterns. TTL deletes old items with zero code — the exam's 'expire sessions automatically' answer.

pitfalls: Using scan for frequent queries — design a GSI instead; scans read the whole table.
LSI after the fact — LSIs can only be created at table creation; GSIs anytime.
Hot partitions from monotonic keys (timestamps) — prefix with randomness to spread write load.
lessons.try_it: Create a table with a GSI, insert 100 items, and query via the GSI instead of scanning.

lessons.title: KMS: Keys, Policies, and Envelope Encryption
concepts: KMS manages symmetric/asymmetric keys; AWS-managed, customer-managed (CMK, full policy control + rotation), and CloudHSM (dedicated hardware, you own the keys).
Envelope encryption: data key encrypts data, KMS key encrypts the data key — you never handle the master key directly.
Key policies control who can use/manage the key — separate from IAM policies; cross-account requires both key policy and IAM to allow.
Automatic annual rotation for CMKs; imported key material for compliance-driven rotation schedules.

example.code:
aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/app-key --plaintext fileb://secret.bin \
  --output text --query CiphertextBlob | base64 -d > secret.enc
aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://secret.enc --output text --query Plaintext | base64 -d
example.walkthrough: For large data, generate a data key, encrypt locally, store the encrypted data key alongside. That is envelope encryption — the pattern behind S3 SSE-KMS and EBS encryption.

pitfalls: Granting IAM kms:* without key policy access — cross-account fails unless the key policy also allows.
Deleting a KMS key immediately — use scheduled deletion (7-30 days) so dependent data can be re-encrypted.
Using KMS for high-throughput per-record encryption — costs explode; use data keys instead.
lessons.try_it: Create a CMK with a key policy, encrypt a file, and try decrypting from another IAM user.

lessons.title: S3 Security: Policies, Block Public Access, and Encryption
concepts: Block Public Access (account + bucket level) overrides any policy that would expose data — enable it everywhere unless a bucket is intentionally public.
Bucket policies (resource-based) vs IAM policies (identity-based) vs ACLs (legacy, disable with Object Ownership = BucketOwnerEnforced).
Encryption: SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS-managed), SSE-KMS (your keys, audit trail, extra cost), SSE-C (you manage keys), client-side. Bucket default encryption applies to all new objects.
Access Points and Access Points for directories simplify per-application access; presigned URLs grant temporary access without IAM identities.

example.code:
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket app-data \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"
aws s3 presign s3://app-data/report.pdf --expires-in 3600
example.walkthrough: Block Public Access first, then share via presigned URLs for temporary access. Exam pattern: 'share privately without IAM users' → presigned URL.

pitfalls: Relying on ACLs in new designs — disable them with BucketOwnerEnforced and use policies.
Choosing SSE-S3 when the requirement demands key rotation audit trails — that is SSE-KMS.
Forgetting Block Public Access is evaluated before bucket policies — a 'public' bucket policy fails silently under BPA.
lessons.try_it: Enable BPA on a bucket, then generate a presigned URL and confirm it works while the bucket stays private.

lessons.title: CloudTrail, Config, and Auditability
concepts: CloudTrail logs every API call (management events free, data events paid) — the 'who did what' record. Multi-region trails + log file validation + KMS encryption for compliance.
Config records configuration history and evaluates rules (managed + custom Lambda) — 'is it compliant right now' vs CloudTrail's 'what changed'.
Org trails aggregate to a central security account; CloudTrail Insights detect unusual API activity.
Athena queries on CloudTrail S3 logs answer forensic questions without a SIEM.

example.code:
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail --s3-bucket-name audit-logs \
  --is-multi-region-trail --enable-log-file-validation --kms-key-id alias/audit
aws configservice put-config-rule --config-rule '{"ConfigRuleName":"s3-encrypted",
  "Source":{"Owner":"AWS","SourceIdentifier":"S3_BUCKET_SERVER_SIDE_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED"}}'
example.walkthrough: Trail for history, Config rule for current-state compliance. Exam pairing: 'detect unauthorized changes' → CloudTrail; 'ensure buckets stay encrypted' → Config rule + auto-remediation.

pitfalls: Single-region trail missing global service events — use multi-region trails.
No log file validation — tampered logs go undetected; always enable it for audit questions.
Confusing Config (state) with CloudTrail (activity) — questions test exactly this distinction.
lessons.try_it: Query last week's ConsoleLogin failures with Athena over CloudTrail logs.

lessons.title: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
concepts: Secrets Manager: automatic rotation (RDS, Redshift, DocumentDB native), cross-account access, per-secret cost. For credentials that must rotate.
Parameter Store (Standard free, Advanced paid): hierarchies (/prod/db/password), SecureString with KMS, no native rotation — pair with Lambda for custom rotation.
Never hardcode secrets; inject at runtime via environment or SDK. Rotation Lambdas follow the 4-step rotation pattern.
Exam rule of thumb: needs rotation → Secrets Manager; simple config values → Parameter Store.

example.code:
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db/creds \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:...:function:rotator \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30
example.walkthrough: Rotation keeps two credential versions live during the swap so apps never break. 'Rotate database passwords every 30 days automatically' → Secrets Manager.

pitfalls: Storing secrets in environment variables in plaintext — use Secrets Manager references instead.
Choosing Parameter Store for auto-rotating DB credentials — it has no native rotation.
Forgetting apps must handle the rotation window — use the staged AWSCURRENT/AWSPREVIOUS versions.
lessons.try_it: Store a secret, enable rotation, and watch the version stages change.

lessons.title: Glue, Athena, and Serverless Analytics
concepts: Glue Crawlers infer schema into the Data Catalog; ETL jobs (Spark) transform; DataBrew for visual prep; bookmarks track processed files.
Athena queries S3 directly with SQL (Presto/Trino) — pay per TB scanned; partition + Parquet + compression to cut cost 10-100x.
Lake Formation adds fine-grained access control on the catalog; governed tables give ACID transactions on S3.
Redshift Serverless for data warehousing without clusters; Spectrum queries S3 from Redshift.

example.code:
-- Athena: partition pruning + columnar = cheap
SELECT date, COUNT(*) FROM logs
WHERE year='2026' AND month='10'   -- partitions
  AND status >= 500                 -- only needed columns
GROUP BY date;
example.walkthrough: Same query on CSV vs partitioned Parquet: 100x cost difference. 'Ad-hoc SQL on S3, minimize cost' → Athena + Parquet + partitions.

pitfalls: Querying raw JSON logs in Athena without partitioning — full scans on every query.
Skipping the crawler and hand-maintaining schemas — crawlers keep the catalog fresh.
Using Redshift provisioned for sporadic queries — Serverless or Athena fit better.
lessons.try_it: Convert JSON logs to partitioned Parquet with Glue, then compare Athena scan sizes.

lessons.title: S3: Buckets, Objects, and Storage Classes
concepts: S3 is object storage: buckets (globally unique names, regional) hold objects (key + data + metadata), 11 nines of durability via multi-AZ replication.
Storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering (auto), Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive. Lifecycle policies move objects down tiers automatically.
Versioning + MFA Delete protect against overwrites; Object Lock gives WORM compliance; Replication (CRR/SRR) copies across regions/accounts.
S3 Express One Zone is single-AZ, millisecond latency, for hot temporary data — different durability model, know when it fits.

example.code:
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket logs --lifecycle-configuration '{
 "Rules":[{"ID":"age-out","Status":"Enabled","Filter":{"Prefix":""},
 "Transitions":[{"Days":30,"StorageClass":"STANDARD_IA"},{"Days":90,"StorageClass":"GLACIER"}],
 "Expiration":{"Days":2555}}]}'
example.walkthrough: Lifecycle rules are the exam's cost-optimization lever for S3: hot → IA at 30 days → Glacier at 90 → expire at 7 years. Intelligent-Tiering automates this when access is unpredictable.

pitfalls: Using Standard for 7-year-old logs — lifecycle to Glacier/Deep Archive is the expected answer.
Forgetting bucket names are globally unique — 'bucket already exists' in another account still blocks you.
Enabling versioning after data loss — it must be on before the overwrite to help.
lessons.try_it: Create a bucket, enable versioning, upload a file twice, and list both versions.

lessons.title: API Gateway: Managed APIs
concepts: REST APIs (full features: usage plans, API keys, caching), HTTP APIs (cheaper, faster, JWT auth), WebSocket APIs (bidirectional).
Stages + deployments version your API; canary deployments shift traffic gradually; throttling + quotas protect backends.
Auth: IAM, Cognito user pools/authorizers, Lambda authorizers, mTLS. Private APIs via VPC endpoints + resource policies.
Direct integrations skip Lambda for S3/DynamoDB/SQS — cheaper and faster for simple CRUD.

example.code:
aws apigatewayv2 create-api --name orders --protocol-type HTTP \
  --target arn:aws:lambda:...:function:orders
aws apigatewayv2 create-stage --api-id abc123 --stage-name prod --auto-deploy
example.walkthrough: HTTP API + Lambda target + JWT authorizer = production API in minutes. 'Serverless REST API with auth' → API Gateway + Cognito/Lambda authorizer.

pitfalls: Using REST API when HTTP API suffices — 70% cheaper for proxy integrations.
No throttling on public APIs — one abusive client can cascade; set route throttles.
Forgetting deployment after changes on REST APIs — HTTP APIs auto-deploy, REST needs explicit deploy.
lessons.try_it: Build an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer fronting a Lambda function.

lessons.title: CloudFront: Global CDN
concepts: CDN with 400+ edge locations: caches content near users, terminates TLS at edge, integrates with WAF, Shield, and Lambda@Edge/CloudFront Functions.
Origins: S3 (use OAC — Origin Access Control), ALB, EC2, or custom. Behaviors route path patterns to different origins/cache policies.
Signed URLs/cookies restrict content; Field-level encryption protects sensitive fields; Origin Shield adds a regional caching layer.
Invalidations cost after 1,000 free/month — versioned filenames beat invalidations for deployments.

example.code:
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123 --paths "/index.html"
# better: deploy as /app-v2.js and update references (no invalidation needed)
example.walkthrough: OAC-secured S3 origin + behaviors for /api/* → ALB. Exam pattern: 'serve private S3 content globally with low latency' → CloudFront + OAC + signed URLs.

pitfalls: Using OAI (legacy) instead of OAC for S3 origins — OAC supports SSE-KMS and is the current answer.
Invalidating /* on every deploy — version assets instead; invalidations are slow and billed.
Forgetting CloudFront is global but the distribution config propagates in minutes — plan deploys accordingly.
lessons.try_it: Put CloudFront in front of a private S3 bucket with OAC and test signed URL access.

lessons.title: AWS Organizations, OUs, and SCPs
concepts: Organizations consolidates billing and policy control: one management account, member accounts grouped into OUs, consolidated billing with volume discounts.
Service Control Policies (SCPs) are guardrails attached to OUs/accounts — they set the maximum permissions, and they do not grant anything by themselves.

SCPs require explicit allow-listing mindset: with FullAWSAccess removed, you must allow each service you want usable. Default FullAWSAccess attached everywhere means SCPs only restrict when you add deny statements.
Control Tower builds a landing zone on top of Organizations with preconfigured OUs (Security, Sandbox), guardrails, and account vending.

example.walkthrough: This SCP denies leaving the org for every account it attaches to — including administrators. Guardrails like this are why exam answers prefer SCPs over asking every team to behave.

pitfalls: Thinking SCPs grant permissions — they only filter; identity policies still do the granting.
Attaching an SCP to the management account — SCPs do not apply to the management account, a favorite exam trap.
Forgetting SCPs affect the root user of member accounts too.
lessons.try_it: Design an OU tree for prod/dev/sandbox and list one SCP per OU.

lessons.title: GuardDuty and Threat Detection
concepts: GuardDuty is ML-based threat detection on CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs — no agents, one-click enable, findings to Security Hub/EventBridge.
Findings severities: low/medium/high/critical; auto-remediation via EventBridge → Lambda (e.g., isolate instance, revoke keys).
Inspector scans EC2/EKS/Lambda for CVEs and network reachability; Macie finds PII in S3 with ML; Detective graphs investigations.
Security Hub aggregates all findings into CIS/PCI standards views with automated checks.

example.code:
aws guardduty create-detector --enable
aws events put-rule --name gd-crypto --event-pattern '{
 "source":["aws.guardduty"],"detail":{"type":[{"prefix":"CryptoCurrency"}]}}'
# target: Lambda that revokes the compromised access key
example.walkthrough: GuardDuty detects mining → EventBridge matches → Lambda revokes keys automatically. 'Detect and respond to threats without agents' → GuardDuty + EventBridge + Lambda.

pitfalls: Installing agents for GuardDuty — it is agentless; that is Inspector/SSM.
Ignoring the 30-day free trial scoping — enable per-account/region deliberately in orgs.
Treating findings as prevention — GuardDuty detects; WAF/Security Groups prevent.
lessons.try_it: Enable GuardDuty, generate a sample finding, and build the EventBridge auto-remediation.

lessons.title: Federation: SSO, SAML, and Identity Center
concepts: Federation lets users authenticate with an external identity provider (corporate AD, Okta, Google) and receive temporary AWS credentials — no IAM users to manage.
IAM Identity Center is the AWS-native SSO: connect your IdP once, assign permission sets to accounts and OUs, users get one portal for everything.
SAML 2.0 and OIDC are the two federation protocols. SAML is typical for workforce SSO; OIDC is typical for web/mobile apps and for GitHub Actions → AWS via IAM Roles Anywhere patterns.
Permission sets in Identity Center map to IAM policies deployed into each target account automatically — one change propagates everywhere.

example.code:
aws sso-admin create-permission-set --instance-arn <instance> \
  --name ReadOnlyPlus --session-duration PT4H
aws sso-admin attach-managed-policy-to-permission-set \
  --instance-arn <instance> --permission-set-arn <ps> \
  --managed-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess
example.walkthrough: Create a permission set once in Identity Center, attach policies, then assign it to groups per account. New account joins the org? Assign the same permission sets — zero per-account IAM work.

pitfalls: Creating IAM users for employees when Identity Center federation is available — the exam treats this as an anti-pattern.
Forgetting session duration limits on permission sets (max 12 hours) in questions about long-running jobs.
Mixing up SAML (workforce) and OIDC (applications) use cases.
lessons.try_it: Sketch how a 50-account org onboards a new engineer: IdP group → permission set → account assignments.

lessons.title: CloudFormation: Infrastructure as Code
concepts: Declarative templates (YAML/JSON): stacks create/update/delete resources as a unit; change sets preview; drift detection finds manual changes.
Parameters + Mappings + Conditions make templates reusable; intrinsic functions (Ref, Fn::Sub, Fn::ImportValue) wire resources together.
Nested stacks and StackSets deploy across accounts/regions; Service Catalog packages approved templates for teams.
DeletionPolicy Retain keeps data resources on stack delete; rollback on failure is default — use --disable-rollback only for debugging.

example.code:
Resources:
  WebBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault: {SSEAlgorithm: AES256}
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
example.walkthrough: Every S3 bucket in the template gets encryption + BPA by construction — compliance as code. 'Enforce standards across teams' → CloudFormation + StackSets + Service Catalog.

pitfalls: Deleting stacks with databases and no DeletionPolicy — data loss; always Retain stateful resources.
Hardcoding values instead of parameters — templates must be environment-agnostic.
Ignoring drift — manual console changes break the next update; detect and remediate.
lessons.try_it: Write a template for a VPC + 2 subnets, deploy, then detect drift after a manual change.

lessons.title: DMS and Database Migration
concepts: DMS migrates with minimal downtime: full load + CDC; homogeneous (same engine) or heterogeneous (Oracle→Postgres via SCT schema conversion).
Replication instance sizing matters; tasks have table mappings/filters; DMS Fleet Advisor rightsizes targets.
Validate with data validation and CloudWatch metrics; cutover during low-traffic windows after lag ≈ 0.
For zero-downtime: DMS ongoing replication + dual-write period + verification, then cutover.

example.code:
aws dms create-replication-task --replication-task-identifier ora2pg \
  --source-endpoint-arn <ora> --target-endpoint-arn <pg> \
  --migration-type full-load-and-cdc --table-mappings file://tables.json
example.walkthrough: Full load seeds, CDC keeps up, lag hits zero → cutover. 'Migrate Oracle to Aurora Postgres with minimal downtime' → SCT + DMS full-load-and-cdc.

pitfalls: Migrating LOBs without full-LOB mode — truncated data; choose limited vs full LOB deliberately.
No validation — always enable DMS data validation for heterogeneous migrations.
Undersized replication instance — CDC lag grows and cutover never arrives.
lessons.try_it: Set up a DMS task with a table filter and watch CDC latency metrics.

lessons.title: SQS: Decoupling with Queues
concepts: SQS decouples producers/consumers: standard (unlimited throughput, best-effort order) vs FIFO (300 TPS batched, strict order, dedup).
Visibility timeout hides messages while processing; if the consumer fails, the message reappears — design idempotent consumers.
DLQs capture poison messages after maxReceiveCount; long polling (20s) cuts cost and latency vs short polling.
Delay queues postpone delivery; message timers per-message; 256KB max (use S3 for larger payloads via extended client).

example.code:
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders.fifo \
  --attributes '{"FifoQueue":"true","ContentBasedDeduplication":"true",
  "VisibilityTimeout":"60","RedrivePolicy":"{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"arn:aws:sqs:...:orders-dlq\",\"maxReceiveCount\":3}"}'
example.walkthrough: FIFO + DLQ: ordered processing, poison messages quarantined after 3 tries. 'Decouple with guaranteed order' → SQS FIFO.

pitfalls: Standard queue for order-dependent workflows — FIFO exists for exactly this.
Visibility timeout shorter than processing time — duplicates flood the consumer.
No DLQ — poison messages loop forever, burning money.
lessons.try_it: Send 10 messages, kill the consumer mid-batch, and watch redelivery.

lessons.title: DataSync: Online Data Transfer
concepts: DataSync moves data between on-prem/NFS/SMB/HDFS and S3/EFS/FSx (and cloud-to-cloud): scheduled, incremental, with integrity verification.
Agents on-prem; bandwidth throttling; task reports detail every file outcome.
Use for migrations, archiving, and replication — 10x faster than scripts via parallel transfers.
For offline petabytes, Snowball Edge is the answer; DataSync is the online counterpart.

example.code:
aws datasync create-task --source-location-arn <nfs> \
  --destination-location-arn <s3> --options '{"VerifyMode":"POINT_IN_TIME_CONSISTENT"}'
aws datasync start-task-execution --task-arn <task>
example.walkthrough: Locations → task → schedule. Verification catches bit-rot in flight. 'Migrate 50TB NAS to S3 online' → DataSync.

pitfalls: No verification mode — silent corruption transfers cleanly.
Unthrottled during business hours — saturates the WAN; schedule/throttle.
Forgetting task reports — failures hide without per-file reporting.
lessons.try_it: Sync a test share and verify with the task report.

lessons.title: Transfer Family: Managed SFTP/FTPS
concepts: Managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP servers backed by S3 or EFS — no servers to run; pay per endpoint-hour + data.
Auth: service-managed, or custom IdP via API Gateway/Lambda, or AD/LDAP.
Workflows: post-upload processing (decrypt, tag, copy) without Lambda glue.
Endpoints: public or VPC-hosted (private); security policies control ciphers/protocols.

example.code:
aws transfer create-server --endpoint-type VPC --protocols SFTP \
  --identity-provider-type API_GATEWAY --url https://auth.example.com
example.walkthrough: Partners keep their SFTP clients; files land in S3 with workflows attached. 'Replace legacy SFTP server' → Transfer Family.

pitfalls: Public endpoint when partners have fixed IPs — VPC endpoint + allowlisting is tighter.
No workflow on upload — files sit unprocessed; attach post-upload actions.
Weak ciphers allowed — set a strict security policy.
lessons.try_it: Stand up an SFTP server with a workflow that tags uploads by partner.

lessons.title: EBS Volumes: Types, Snapshots, and Performance
concepts: EBS is AZ-scoped block storage: gp3 (baseline 3,000 IOPS, cheapest general), io2 (sub-ms, 99.999% durability, critical DBs), st1/sc1 (throughput HDDs for big sequential), standard (legacy).
gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size — the cost-optimization answer over gp2/io1 in most questions.
Snapshots are incremental, stored in S3, and can seed new volumes/AZs; DLM automates snapshot lifecycles; Fast Snapshot Restore removes first-use latency.
Encrypted by default can be enforced; you can resize live but must extend the filesystem inside the OS afterward.

example.code:
aws ec2 create-volume --availability-zone us-east-1a --size 100 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 5000 --throughput 250 --encrypted
example.walkthrough: gp3 decouples IOPS/throughput from size — provision exactly what the workload needs instead of overbuying gigabytes for performance like gp2 forced you to.

pitfalls: Assuming EBS is multi-AZ — it is not; snapshots/AMIs are the cross-AZ mechanism.
Forgetting to extend the filesystem after resizing — the volume grows but the OS cannot see it.
Using io2 where gp3 suffices — 3x the cost for latency the app never notices.
lessons.try_it: Snapshot a volume, restore it in another AZ, and attach it to a new instance.

lessons.title: Athena: Performance and Governance
concepts: Engine v3 (Trino): better performance; provisioned capacity for predictable workloads; federated queries to non-S3 sources.
Workgroups: per-team limits, query history, cost allocation tags; primary workgroup is not for production.
Prepared statements prevent SQL injection in dashboards; views + Lake Formation for fine-grained access.
Result reuse and CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS) materialize expensive queries.

example.code:
-- CTAS: pay once, query many
CREATE TABLE curated.daily WITH (
  format='PARQUET', partitioned_by=ARRAY['dt'],
  external_location='s3://curated/daily/')
AS SELECT * FROM raw.events WHERE dt > current_date - interval '7' day;
example.walkthrough: CTAS converts expensive raw scans into cheap curated tables. 'Athena too slow/expensive' → CTAS + partitions + workgroup limits.

pitfalls: Everyone on the primary workgroup — no limits, no cost allocation.
No CTAS for repeated queries — paying full scan every time.
String-concatenated SQL in apps — use prepared statements.
lessons.try_it: Convert a repeated dashboard query to CTAS and compare cost.

lessons.title: OpenSearch: Search and Analytics
concepts: Managed OpenSearch/Elasticsearch: full-text search, log analytics, SIEM dashboards; domains with dedicated master nodes for prod.
UltraWarm/cold tiers for aging log data; ISM policies automate rollover/delete.
Fine-grained access control + SAML; encryption at rest/in transit; VPC deployment for isolation.
Serverless option for variable workloads — no cluster sizing.

example.code:
aws opensearch create-domain --domain-name logs --engine-version OpenSearch_2.11 \
  --cluster-config '{"InstanceType":"m6g.large.search","InstanceCount":3,"DedicatedMasterEnabled":true}' \
  --ebs-options '{"EBSEnabled":true,"VolumeSize":100}'
example.walkthrough: 3 data + 3 master for prod; ISM moves old indices to UltraWarm. 'Centralized log search' → OpenSearch + ISM lifecycle.

pitfalls: Single-AZ domain for prod — node failure = outage; multi-AZ minimum.
No ISM policy — hot storage fills with ancient indices.
Public endpoint without FGAC — open search is a breach waiting to happen.
lessons.try_it: Create an ISM policy rolling daily indices to UltraWarm after 7 days.

lessons.title: AWS Backup: Centralized Protection
concepts: One console for EC2, RDS, EFS, S3, DynamoDB backups: plans (frequency/retention), vaults, vault lock (WORM).
Cross-region and cross-account copy for DR; legal hold for litigation.
Backup Audit Manager checks compliance (e.g., 'all RDS have 7-day retention').
Restore testing plans validate recoverability automatically.

example.code:
aws backup create-backup-plan --backup-plan '{"BackupPlanName":"prod",
 "Rules":[{"RuleName":"daily","TargetBackupVaultName":"prod-vault",
 "ScheduleExpression":"cron(0 2 * * ? *)","Lifecycle":{"DeleteAfterDays":35}}]}'
example.walkthrough: Tag-based assignment: tag resources, plans pick them up. 'Prove backups work' → restore testing plans.

pitfalls: No vault lock — ransomware deletes backups; WORM is the point.
Same-region only — regional events take data + backups.
Never testing restores — untested backup is a hope.
lessons.try_it: Enable vault lock and attempt a (denied) early deletion.

lessons.title: EFS and Shared File Storage
concepts: EFS is regional NFS shared by thousands of clients across AZs — lift-and-shift shared filesystems, CMS content, home directories.
Performance modes: General Purpose (default, low latency) vs Max I/O (higher throughput, slightly higher latency); Throughput modes: Bursting, Provisioned, Elastic.
Lifecycle management moves cold files to Infrequent Access automatically; mount targets (one per AZ) + security groups control access.
FSx family: Windows File Server (SMB/AD), Lustre (HPC/ML scratch), NetApp ONTAP (NFS/SMB/iSCSI multiprotocol), OpenZFS.

example.code:
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-12345678:/ /mnt/efs
# /etc/fstab for persistence:
fs-12345678:/ /mnt/efs efs _netdev,tls 0 0
example.walkthrough: One mount target per AZ, TLS in transit, lifecycle policy to IA. Exam signal: 'shared file access across AZs/instances' → EFS; 'Windows SMB with AD' → FSx for Windows.

pitfalls: Using EBS for multi-instance shared writes — EBS is single-attach (mostly); EFS/FSx share.
Mounting without TLS on untrusted networks — always use the tls option in exam answers.
Picking Max I/O mode by default — General Purpose has lower per-operation latency for typical workloads.
lessons.try_it: Mount an EFS filesystem from two instances and write a file from one, read from the other.

lessons.title: CloudWatch: Metrics, Logs, and Alarms
concepts: Metrics (1s-1d granularity, 15-month retention), Logs (centralized, Insights query language, metric filters), Alarms (threshold/composite/anomaly).
Dashboards visualize; Contributor Insights finds top talkers; Synthetics canaries probe endpoints; RUM captures real-user frontend data.
Alarms → SNS → auto-remediation (Lambda/SSM) or paging; composite alarms reduce noise by combining states.
Embedded Metric Format lets Lambda/ECS emit custom metrics via logs without PutMetricData calls.

example.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name high-cpu \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average \
  --period 300 --threshold 80 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 2 --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:...:ops
example.walkthrough: Metric → alarm → SNS → action. Exam pattern: 'alert and auto-remediate' → CloudWatch alarm + EventBridge/SSM automation.

pitfalls: Alarming on raw metrics without dimensions — aggregate alarms hide the failing instance.
No composite alarms — alert fatigue from 50 firing alarms instead of one 'service degraded'.
Forgetting log retention defaults to never expire — set retention to control cost.
lessons.try_it: Create a metric filter on logs that counts 500 errors and alarm on it.

lessons.title: EMR Serverless and Studio
concepts: EMR Serverless: Spark/Hive without clusters — pay per vCPU-hour; auto scales; same APIs as EMR.
EMR on EKS for Kubernetes-native Spark; EMR Studio notebooks for interactive dev.
Use for batch ETL, ML preprocessing, log processing at scale.
Cost levers: pre-initialized capacity for steady jobs, spot workers where supported.

example.code:
aws emr-serverless create-application --name etl --release-label emr-7.0.0 --type SPARK
aws emr-serverless start-job-run --application-id <app> --execution-role-arn <role> \
  --job-driver '{"sparkSubmit":{"entryPoint":"s3://code/etl.py"}}'
example.walkthrough: Submit Spark jobs with no cluster to babysit. 'Run Spark without infrastructure' → EMR Serverless.

pitfalls: Provisioned EMR for sporadic jobs — Serverless removes idle cost.
No pre-initialized capacity for latency-sensitive jobs — cold starts hurt.
Oversized workers — right-size vCPU/memory per job.
lessons.try_it: Run a Spark job serverless and compare cost to a transient cluster.

lessons.title: X-Ray: Distributed Tracing
concepts: X-Ray traces requests across services: segments (per service) and subsegments (per call), visualized as service maps showing latency contributors.
Instrument with SDKs (automatic for AWS SDK calls) or the daemon; sampling rules control cost (e.g., 5% + all errors).
Annotations (indexed, searchable) vs metadata (not indexed); filter expressions find slow traces fast.
ServiceLens combines X-Ray + CloudWatch metrics/logs for unified observability.

example.walkthrough: Decorate the slow function; the trace shows exactly which downstream call burns time. 'Find the slow microservice' → X-Ray service map.

pitfalls: 100% sampling in production — cost explosion; sample aggressively, keep errors.
No annotations on key attributes — traces exist but are unsearchable.
Tracing without the daemon/security group — UDP 2000 must reach the daemon.
lessons.try_it: Instrument one endpoint and find its p99 contributor in the service map.

lessons.title: Containers on AWS: ECS, Fargate, and EKS
concepts: ECS is AWS-native orchestration (tasks + services); Fargate removes the EC2 cluster to manage; EKS is managed Kubernetes for portability.
Choose Fargate for simplicity and per-second billing; EC2 launch type when you need GPU, special networking, or daemon control.
EKS with managed node groups or Fargate profiles; IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) gives pods scoped AWS permissions via OIDC.
Service discovery with Cloud Map, load balancing via ALB/NLB target groups in ip or instance mode.

example.code:
aws ecs register-task-definition --family web \
  --network-mode awsvpc --requires-compatibilities FARGATE \
  --cpu 256 --memory 512 --container-definitions file://c.json
aws ecs create-service --cluster prod --service-name web --task-definition web --desired-count 3
example.walkthrough: Fargate + awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI and security group — microsegmentation without managing hosts. That is the exam's preferred pattern for 'run containers without servers.'

pitfalls: Picking EKS when the team has no Kubernetes experience and ECS/Fargate would do — match the service to the org.
Forgetting IRSA and giving nodes broad instance-profile permissions — pods inherit too much.
Using instance-mode targets with Fargate tasks — Fargate requires ip mode.
lessons.try_it: Run an nginx Fargate service behind an ALB with 2 tasks across 2 AZs.

lessons.title: IAM Users, Groups, and Least Privilege
concepts: IAM is global and free: users, groups, and roles exist once per account, not per region. Policies are JSON documents that allow or deny actions on resources.
Default deny: everything is denied unless an identity policy, resource policy, or permission boundary explicitly allows it. An explicit deny in any policy always wins.
Groups hold permissions, users go in groups — never attach policies directly to users in production. Roles are assumed temporarily and are the only way to grant cross-account or service access.
Root user must be locked down: enable MFA, never create access keys for root, and use it only for account-level tasks like changing support plans.

example.code:
aws iam create-group --group-name Developers
aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name Developers \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name alice --group-name Developers
example.walkthrough: Create a group, attach a managed policy once, then add users to the group. When someone changes teams you move one membership instead of editing five policies — this is the pattern exam questions reward.

pitfalls: Attaching AdministratorAccess to users directly instead of using groups and roles — unmanageable and fails least-privilege questions.
Forgetting that IAM is global: creating the same user per region is a classic distractor in design questions.
Leaving the root account without MFA — the single most penalized answer in security scenarios.
lessons.try_it: In the console, create a group with PowerUserAccess, add a test user, and confirm the user cannot touch IAM itself.

lessons.title: Macie: PII Discovery in S3
concepts: Macie uses ML to find PII/PHI in S3: managed identifiers (100+ types) + custom identifiers (regex); findings to Security Hub/EventBridge.
Discovery jobs: one-time, scheduled, or automated (sensitive data discovery across the org); sampling keeps cost proportional.
Findings include bucket, object, and identifier type — enough to scope remediation without viewing the data.
Pair with S3 Block Public Access and Lake Formation for the find → fix → prevent loop.

example.code:
aws macie2 create-classification-job --job-type ONE_TIME \
  --s3-job-definition '{"BucketDefinitions":[{"AccountId":"123456789012","Buckets":["data-lake"]}]}' \
  --managed-data-identifier-selector ALL
example.walkthrough: Run discovery, triage findings by severity, remediate buckets, schedule recurring jobs. 'Find PII at scale' → Macie.

pitfalls: Scanning everything at full depth immediately — cost surprise; sample first, then target.
Findings without remediation workflow — discovery without action is theater.
Ignoring custom identifiers for org-specific data formats.
lessons.try_it: Run a one-time job on a test bucket with planted PII and review findings.

lessons.title: Config: Advanced Compliance Patterns
concepts: Conformance packs bundle rules + remediation for frameworks (CIS, PCI); aggregators give org-wide compliance views.
Custom Lambda rules evaluate anything the managed rules miss; periodic vs configuration-change triggers.
Remediation via SSM Automation documents; auto-remediation for safe fixes, manual for risky ones.
Config timeline is forensic gold: every change with who/when.

example.code:
aws configservice put-remediation-configurations --config-rule-name s3-encrypted \
  --remediation-configurations '[{"TargetType":"SSM_DOCUMENT",
  "TargetId":"AWS-EnableS3BucketEncryption","Automatic":true,"MaximumAutomaticAttempts":3}]'
example.walkthrough: Rule detects, SSM fixes, Config verifies — closed loop. 'Continuously enforce encryption' → Config rule + auto-remediation.

pitfalls: Auto-remediation on destructive actions — gate risky fixes behind approval.
No aggregator — per-region views hide org-wide drift.
Custom rules without tests — false positives erode trust.
lessons.try_it: Deploy a conformance pack and auto-remediate one rule.

lessons.title: Control Tower: Landing Zone Governance
concepts: Control Tower automates the multi-account baseline: Security and Sandbox OUs, centralized logging/audit accounts, guardrails (preventive SCPs + detective Config).
Account Factory vends new accounts with baselines applied; customization via CfCT (Customizations for Control Tower) or AFT (Account Factory for Terraform).
Guardrails: mandatory (e.g., no public S3), strongly recommended, elective — mapped to compliance frameworks.
Drift on enrolled accounts is detected; re-register to remediate.

example.code:
# Account Factory request (via Service Catalog):
# Product: AWS Control Tower Account Factory
# Parameters: AccountName, SSOUserEmail, ManagedOrganizationalUnit
# Result: account with baselines + guardrails in ~30 min
example.walkthrough: New team? One factory request → compliant account. 'Standardize 50 accounts' → Control Tower, not hand-built orgs.

pitfalls: Hand-building what Control Tower automates — drift and inconsistency follow.
Ignoring guardrail drift — enrolled accounts can still drift; monitor it.
No customization pipeline — CfCT/AFT keeps baselines in code.
lessons.try_it: List the guardrails enabled on your landing zone and map two to CIS controls.

lessons.title: Detective: Investigation Graphs
concepts: Detective builds entity graphs from CloudTrail/VPC/GuradDuty data: which IP touched which role, when — visualized timelines.
No setup beyond enabling; 1-year data retention for investigations.
Use after GuardDuty findings: pivot from finding → entity → full activity graph.
Complements SIEM: fast triage before deep log diving.

example.code:
aws detective create-graph
# then: GuardDuty finding -> 'Investigate in Detective'
# graph shows: IP -> API calls -> roles assumed -> resources touched
example.walkthrough: Finding → graph → scope of compromise in minutes. 'Scope an incident fast' → Detective.

pitfalls: Not enabled before the incident — needs history; enable proactively.
Treating it as prevention — it is investigation, not detection.
Single region — enable where your workloads are.
lessons.try_it: Investigate a sample finding and map the full entity graph.

lessons.title: Inspector: Continuous Vulnerability Scanning
concepts: Inspector v2 scans EC2 (via SSM agent), ECR images, and Lambda for CVEs + network reachability; scores with Inspector risk score.
Continuous scanning on push/schedule; findings to Security Hub; suppressions for accepted risks.
CIS benchmark assessments for OS hardening; Lambda code scanning for vulnerabilities.
Suppression rules need expiry and justification — accepted risk, not ignored risk.

example.code:
aws inspector2 enable --resource-types EC2 ECR LAMBDA
aws inspector2 list-findings --filter-criteria '{"severity":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"CRITICAL"}]}'
example.walkthrough: Enable once per org (delegated admin); findings flow to Security Hub. 'Continuous CVE scanning without agents to manage' → Inspector (SSM agent required on EC2).

pitfalls: EC2 without SSM agent — no scan coverage; the agent is the prerequisite.
Treating all findings equally — prioritize by Inspector score + exploitability.
No suppression process — teams drown in accepted-risk noise.
lessons.try_it: Enable Inspector, find one critical CVE, patch, and verify the finding closes.

lessons.title: SNS: Pub/Sub Messaging
concepts: SNS is pub/sub: topics fan out to SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS, mobile push. One message → many subscribers, at-least-once delivery.
FIFO topics preserve order and deduplicate (with SQS FIFO subscribers); standard topics maximize throughput without ordering.
Message filtering lets subscribers receive only matching messages — filter policies on attributes reduce noise and cost.
Access control via topic policies; encryption with SSE; dead-letter queues on subscriptions for failed deliveries.

example.code:
aws sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:...:alerts \
  --message "CPU critical" --message-attributes '{"severity":{"DataType":"String","StringValue":"critical"}}'
example.walkthrough: Publish once with attributes; each subscription filters what it wants. 'Notify many systems from one event' → SNS fan-out.

pitfalls: Using SNS for ordered processing — use FIFO topics or SQS FIFO instead.
Expecting exactly-once — SNS is at-least-once; subscribers must be idempotent.
No filtering: every subscriber gets everything — filter policies fix this.
lessons.try_it: Create a topic with email + SQS subscriptions and different filter policies.

lessons.title: Systems Manager: Fleet Operations
concepts: SSM Agent on instances enables: Session Manager (shell without SSH/bastion), Run Command (fleet-wide commands), Patch Manager, State Manager (desired config).
Parameter Store hierarchies for config; Automation runbooks for repeatable workflows; Inventory + Compliance dashboards.
Session Manager logs to S3/CloudWatch — auditable shell access with IAM control instead of key pairs.
Distributor deploys software packages; OpsCenter aggregates operational issues.

example.code:
aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunPatchBaseline \
  --targets '[{"Key":"tag:Env","Values":["prod"]}]' \
  --parameters '{"Operation":["Install"]}'
aws ssm start-session --target i-1234567890abcdef0
example.walkthrough: Patch 500 instances with one command, then open audited sessions without SSH keys. 'Manage fleet without bastions' → Session Manager + IAM.

pitfalls: Opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 for admin access — Session Manager removes the need entirely.
Instances without the SSM agent or instance profile — no agent, no management.
Manual patching per instance — Patch Manager with maintenance windows is the exam answer.
lessons.try_it: Start a Session Manager session to an instance with no SSH key and port 22 closed.

lessons.title: CodePipeline: CI/CD Orchestration
concepts: Stages: Source (CodeCommit/GitHub/S3) → Build (CodeBuild) → Test → Deploy (CodeDeploy/CloudFormation/ECS) → Approval gates between stages.
Artifacts pass between stages via S3; pipeline executions are visible end-to-end; cross-account via roles + KMS keys.
Manual approval actions pause for human sign-off — the exam's 'require approval before prod' answer.
Triggers on push, schedules, or webhooks; pipeline-level variables share config across actions.

example.code:
aws codepipeline create-pipeline --cli-input-json '{
 "pipeline":{"name":"web","roleArn":"arn:aws:iam::...:role/pipeline",
 "stages":[{"name":"Source","actions":[{"name":"src","actionTypeId":
 {"category":"Source","owner":"AWS","provider":"CodeCommit","version":"1"},
 "configuration":{"RepositoryName":"web","BranchName":"main"},"outputArtifacts":[{"name":"src"}]}]}]}}'
example.walkthrough: Source → Build → Manual Approval → Deploy. The approval action is the lever exam questions pull for 'human gate before production'.

pitfalls: No approval before prod deploys — add manual approval actions for regulated flows.
Artifacts too large for the 100MB... use S3 directly for big artifacts; pipeline artifacts have limits.
Single account for everything — cross-account pipelines isolate prod properly.
lessons.try_it: Add a manual approval stage between test and prod in a sample pipeline.

lessons.title: WAF, Shield, and Edge Protection
concepts: WAF: Layer-7 firewall on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway — managed rules (SQLi, XSS, known bad inputs), rate-based rules, custom regex/geo rules, Bot Control.
Shield Standard (free, automatic DDoS) vs Shield Advanced (24/7 DRT, cost protection, advanced metrics) — Advanced is the exam answer for 'enterprise DDoS with support'.
WAF + CloudFront + ALB is the standard web-protection stack; AWS Firewall Manager deploys WAF rules across accounts centrally.
Rate-based rules block IPs exceeding thresholds — the answer to 'brute force login' questions at the edge.

example.code:
aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name app-protect --scope CLOUDFRONT \
  --default-action Allow={} --rules '[{"Name":"rate-limit","Priority":1,
  "Statement":{"RateBasedStatement":{"Limit":2000,"AggregateKeyType":"IP"}},
  "Action":{"Block":{}},"VisibilityConfig":{"SampledRequestsEnabled":true,"CloudWatchMetricsEnabled":true,"MetricName":"rate-limit"}}]'
example.walkthrough: Rate-based rule: >2000 requests/5min from one IP → block. Layer managed SQLi/XSS rules above it. That two-layer WAF is the exam's web-app defense answer.

pitfalls: Putting WAF on EC2 directly — WAF attaches to CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway, not instances.
Expecting Shield Standard to include DRT support — that is Shield Advanced.
Forgetting Firewall Manager for multi-account WAF consistency.
lessons.try_it: Attach AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet to a WAF and test a blocked SQLi payload.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: how to study, AWS Data Engineer exam structure) → Lessons (deep-dives in domain order: Data Ingestion, Data Lakes & Warehouses, Processing Frameworks, Data Governance, Orchestration, Analytics) → Scenarios (multiple-choice drills, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on terminal exercises) → Timed mock (the full DEA-C01 simulation). Each layer assumes the one before.

What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands and the computer prints results — no buttons, no mouse. Cloud CLIs (aws, az) follow the same pattern: service, then action, then flags. You cannot break anything by typing a wrong command in the labs — the worst case is an error message, which is itself information.

The DEA-C01 exam strategy baked into this bootcamp: learn the concept in Lessons, recognize it in Scenarios, execute it in Labs, then prove it under time pressure in the Mock. Skipping straight to the mock is like taking the final before the lectures.

lessons.title: DEA-C01 Exam Structure and Question Patterns
concepts: The DEA-C01 exam is multiple-choice and multiple-response, delivered at a testing center or via online proctoring. Questions are scenario-based: a paragraph of context, then 'what should you do?' — never pure trivia.

Every question has one best answer and three distractors built from common misconceptions. Two answers often look right; the correct one matches the constraint words: 'most cost-effective,' 'least operational overhead,' 'most secure,' 'highly available.'
AWS exams test decision-making, not memorization: expect 'a company needs X with constraints Y and Z' and four architectures. Your job is to map constraints to services.
Flag-and-return: answer what you know fast, flag the hard ones, return with remaining time. Unanswered questions score zero — never leave blanks.

example.code:
Question anatomy:
  Stem: 'A company runs ... The solution must be highly available
         and minimize operational overhead. What should the architect do?'
  Constraint words: HIGHLY AVAILABLE + MINIMIZE OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD
  -> eliminate self-managed options (operational overhead)
  -> eliminate single-AZ options (availability)
  -> pick the managed multi-AZ answer
example.walkthrough: Underline constraint words first, eliminate two distractors, then choose between the last two by re-reading the stem. This mechanical process beats 'gut feeling' consistently.

pitfalls: Answering from real-world habit instead of the exam's best practice — the exam wants the textbook answer, not your team's workaround.
Ignoring constraint words — 'cheapest' vs 'most resilient' flip the correct answer between the same two options.
Changing answers on review without new reasoning — first instincts, backed by elimination, are usually right.
lessons.try_it: Take 5 scenarios in the drills and write down the constraint words before answering.

lessons.title: Hands-On Labs: Building Muscle Memory
concepts: Labs are terminal exercises with automated checks: each step gives you a command to run, and checks verify the result. A hint appears if a check fails — read it, it diagnoses the exact miss.
The lab terminal is a safe sandbox: create, delete, break things. Every exam objective you can DO is one you will not forget under pressure.

For AWS Data Engineer, the highest-value lab skills are the ones questions describe as actions: creating, configuring, verifying, troubleshooting. If a scenario says 'the engineer runs X,' you should have run X in a lab.
Repeat labs you fumble. The second run should take half the time — that speed delta is exam readiness.

example.code:
Lab loop:
  1. Read the objective (what 'done' looks like)
  2. Run each step, observing output (not just copy-paste)
  3. If a check fails, read the hint -- it names the exact gap
  4. Finish, then re-do the lab from memory tomorrow

  Checks are your examiner: green means you actually did it.
example.walkthrough: Do not copy-paste blindly: after each command, ask 'what did that change?' The checks only pass when the real state is correct.

pitfalls: Copy-pasting without reading output — the exam will ask what the output means.
Skipping the failed-check hints — they are the fastest diagnosis you will get anywhere.
Doing each lab once — spaced repetition (day 1, day 3, day 7) locks it in.

lessons.title: Reading Questions Like an Examiner
concepts: Examiners write distractors from real mistakes: the 'almost right' answer that misses one constraint, the 'real-world habit' answer that is not best practice, the 'correct service, wrong feature' answer.
Constraint words decide everything: 'MOST cost-effective,' 'LEAST operational overhead,' 'MOST secure,' 'WITHOUT managing servers,' 'MEET compliance.' Circle them before reading options.
Length is a signal, not noise: long stems hide the one sentence that matters. Read the last sentence first (the actual question), then scan for constraints.
Absolute words ('always,' 'never') are usually wrong; qualified words ('typically,' 'minimize') usually right — but verify against constraints, never as a sole rule.

example.code:
Stem: '...must retain logs for 7 years for compliance, with minimal
 effort. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?'
Parse: constraint = 7-YEAR RETENTION + MINIMAL EFFORT + CHEAPEST
Eliminate: manual pipelines (effort), hot storage for 7 years (cost)
Answer family: lifecycle to archive tier + retention policy
example.walkthrough: Practice this parse on every drill: constraints → eliminate two → decide between two. Speed comes from the mechanical habit.

pitfalls: Reading options before the stem — anchors you to attractive distractors.
Choosing the 'coolest' service instead of the constrained one — exam rewards boring and correct.
Overthinking 'trick' questions — most are straightforward constraint matches.
lessons.try_it: Do 10 scenarios writing only the constraint words first; check if your accuracy rises.

lessons.title: Elimination Tactics That Work
concepts: Two-pass method: pass 1 eliminates options violating any constraint (usually kills 2); pass 2 compares survivors on the remaining constraints.
Service-family elimination: if the stem needs serverless, eliminate every EC2/VM-based option immediately without reading further.
Cost-order elimination: when 'most cost-effective' appears, rank options by managed-ness — more managed usually wins unless a constraint forbids it.
Security-order elimination: when 'most secure,' prefer options with encryption by default, private networking, and least privilege — in that order.

example.code:
Q: '...serverless, lowest cost, event-driven image processing...'
A) EC2 fleet with cron        -> eliminate (not serverless)
B) Lambda + S3 events        -> keep
C) ECS on EC2                -> eliminate (not serverless)
D) Lambda + polling EC2      -> eliminate (polling = waste)
Answer: B in under 20 seconds.
example.walkthrough: Elimination turns 4-option questions into 2-option questions, doubling your odds even when unsure. Drill it until it is reflex.

pitfalls: Eliminating on vibes — every elimination needs a cited constraint from the stem.
Keeping an option because it 'sounds enterprise' — the exam does not grade vibes.
Forgetting to re-read the stem after elimination — the final two need the full context.
lessons.try_it: For the next 15 scenarios, write your two eliminations and reasons before choosing.

lessons.title: Time Management Under Pressure
concepts: Budget per question: total minutes ÷ question count, minus 15 minutes buffer. For a 130-minute, 65-question DEA-C01: ~1m45s each. A 3-minute question is stealing from two others.
The 90-second rule: if you have not eliminated two options in 90 seconds, flag and move on. Hard questions cluster — do not let one sink your pace.
First pass: answer everything you can in under 60 seconds. Second pass: flagged questions with fresh eyes. Third pass: review marked-for-review only.
Never leave blanks: with no penalty for wrong answers, a guess among two survivors is a 50% expected score vs 0% blank.

example.code:
65 questions, 130 minutes:
  Pass 1 (60 min): all sub-60s questions -> ~40 answered
  Pass 2 (40 min): flagged questions -> ~20 answered
  Pass 3 (15 min): review marked -> adjust a few
  Buffer (15 min):  breathing room / technical issues
example.walkthrough: Practice with the mock timer. Your pass-1 speed is the skill — the mock's per-question pacing feedback trains exactly this.

pitfalls: Perfectionism on question 7 — the exam is won on questions 30-65, which you never reach.
No flagging discipline — 'I'll remember to come back' fails under stress; flag explicitly.
Skipping the buffer — technical hiccups happen; plan for them.
lessons.try_it: Run a 20-question drill with a 35-minute timer and enforce the 90-second rule.

lessons.title: Scenario Questions: Multi-Service Design
concepts: Hard questions combine 2-3 services: identify each requirement, map it to a service, then check the combination for conflicts (regions, limits, auth).
Draw the data flow: source → processing → storage → consumer. Wrong answers usually break one arrow (wrong trigger, wrong permission, wrong region).
Permissions are the hidden test: the architecture can be perfect and still wrong if the role/policy is missing. Always ask 'who is allowed to call what?'
Cost and operations are tiebreakers: between two working designs, the exam prefers managed, serverless, and event-driven.

example.code:
Flow check for 'S3 upload -> process -> notify':
  S3 event notification -> Lambda? (permission: s3:Put -> lambda:Invoke?)
  Lambda -> DynamoDB? (execution role allows dynamodb:PutItem?)
  Lambda -> SNS? (role allows sns:Publish?)
  Dead-letter on failure? (SQS DLQ configured?)
  => 4 arrows, 4 permission checks. The distractor breaks exactly one.
example.walkthrough: For every design question, sketch the arrows and label the permission on each. The option with all arrows green is the answer.

pitfalls: Checking services but not permissions — the exam's favorite trap.
Forgetting DLQs/retries on async flows — 'what happens on failure' is always asked.
Regional mismatch — KMS keys, some services, and data residency are regional.
lessons.try_it: Take any 3-service scenario and draw the arrow diagram with permissions labeled.

steps.context: Nightly ETL: extract from sources, transform, load the warehouse, then validate.
items: Transform and clean the extracted records
Validate row counts and publish the data-quality report
Extract changed records from the source systems
Load the transformed data into the warehouse

simulations.debrief: You ordered the ETL correctly: extract, transform, load, then validate. Validation last means the report covers the whole run.

simulations.title: The warehouse is stale
simulations.brief: The 06:00 warehouse refresh never landed and the dashboard shows yesterday's numbers. The orchestrator log is your evidence.

steps.symptom: Warehouse tables are 24h stale; the orchestrator shows the extract stage green, transform red.
evidence:
extract: 1.2M rows staged to s3://ilb-data-raw ... OK
transform: ERROR schema mismatch on column 'amount' (expected INTEGER, got TEXT)
load: skipped (upstream failed)
options: Re-run the whole pipeline — transient errors clear on retry
Inspect the raw staged data: the source changed the 'amount' column type
Drop the warehouse table and reload from scratch
Disable the transform stage so the load can proceed
steps.explain: The log names it: a schema mismatch on 'amount'. The source changed the column type — re-running or skipping transform just repeats or hides the failure. Fix the schema handling first.

steps.symptom: The source now sends 'amount' as TEXT ('2400' instead of 2400).
options: Cast TEXT to INTEGER in the transform with validation for bad values
Change the warehouse column to TEXT to match the source
Ask the source team to revert — pipelines should never adapt
Load the TEXT values and fix them in the dashboard queries
steps.explain: Adapt in the transform with explicit casting and bad-value handling — that is what the transform stage is for. Changing the warehouse type corrupts downstream analytics; dashboard-side fixes hide the problem.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed a schema-drift failure at the right layer: the transform adapts and validates, the warehouse stays clean, and the evidence led every step.

simulations.title: Schema-on-write or schema-on-read?
simulations.brief: The team argues about where to enforce schema: at ingest (strict) or at read (flexible). The workload decides — walk the tree.

steps.text: The new clickstream feed arrives as messy JSON, fields change weekly, and analysts explore it ad hoc. Enforce schema at ingest?

choices.label: Yes — strict schema at ingest keeps everything clean
choices.feedback: Strict ingest schema on a weekly-changing feed means the pipeline breaks weekly. Flexibility matters here.

choices.label: No — land it raw, enforce schema at read time
choices.feedback: Correct — schema-on-read (data lake pattern) absorbs volatile feeds without breaking ingest.

steps.text: The pipeline broke twice this month on new fields. Reconsider:

choices.label: Land raw, enforce at read
choices.feedback: Right — let the lake be flexible and push structure to query time.

steps.text: Now the finance ledger: regulated, audited, downstream reports must reconcile to the cent. Same choice?

choices.label: Schema-on-read again — consistency
choices.feedback: Wrong: regulated financial data needs schema-on-write with validation at ingest. Flexibility here is a compliance violation.

choices.label: Schema-on-write with validation — it is regulated data
choices.feedback: Correct — the workload decides. Volatile exploration data gets schema-on-read; regulated data gets strict schema-on-write.

simulations.debrief: You learned the real rule: there is no single right answer — volatile exploration data wants schema-on-read, regulated data demands schema-on-write.

simulations.title: The crawler that misfires
simulations.brief: The Glue crawler keeps creating a new table per file instead of one table per dataset. Review the crawler config and click the offending lines.

sections.heading: Data Ingestion
items: Kinesis Data Streams — provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. Kinesis Data Firehose is the managed delivery service: it buffers, converts (e.g., to Parquet), and loads streaming data into S3 and other destinations with no consum…

Streaming ingestion — SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service. Data Streams and MSK require consumers; DynamoDB direct PUT isn't a streaming pipeline.
Firehose — Firehose/Data Streams aren't Kafka-compatible; SQS FIFO lacks Kafka's log semantics and retention model.

Managed delivery — amazon MSK provides managed Apache Kafka with Kafka API compatibility, configurable long retention, and exactly-once semantics support. AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints backed by S3 — partners keep their workflow, files land in S3.
Common trap — kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers.
Skipping the key question — which service is built for high-throughput ordered event streams with multiple consumers.
Skipping the key question — which service loads streaming data to destinations with no consumer code.

Kinesis Data Streams — provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service.

sections.heading: Data Lakes & Warehouses
items: Data lakes — an S3-based data lake with the Glue Data Catalog stores all data types in open formats with evolving schemas, serving diverse consumers. The Glue Data Catalog provides a central, queryable metadata store (databases, tables, schemas, partitions) integrated w…
S3 — S3: redshift Spectrum extends Redshift SQL queries to S3 data in place — no loading, paying per query.
Redshift Serverless — Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales warehouse capacity for the workload, paying for usage — ideal for spiky analytics.
Glue Data Catalog — parquet's columnar format lets engines read only the needed columns (plus compression and predicate pushdown), slashing scanned data and cost.
Common trap — S3 with bronze/silver/gold zones + Lake Formation permissions.
Skipping the key question — which architecture handles all data types with evolving schema.
Skipping the key question — which warehouse option scales to zero operationally for spiky use.

An S3-based — An S3-based data lake with the Glue Data Catalog stores all data types in open formats with evolving schemas, serving diverse consumers. A warehouse alone forces schema-on-write; RDS isn't analytics storage; EBS isn't a lake.

sections.heading: Processing Frameworks
items: Glue — is Spark-centric serverless; Lambda isn't for clusters; Athena is serverless SQL, not a framework platform. Incremental processing (e.g., Glue job bookmarks tracking processed offsets) handles only new data each run, keeping runtime flat.

Serverless Spark — AWS Glue provides serverless Spark ETL with auto-scaling workers — no clusters to manage. EMR provides managed clusters with the full big-data ecosystem (Spark, Flink, Presto/Trino) and notebook support.

EMR — always-on EC2 idles at zero; EMR is for cluster analytics, not 200ms functions; bare metal is the opposite of elastic. EMR/Glue clusters idle between queries; Redshift is a provisioned warehouse.

Big data clusters — stream processing (MSK + Flink, or Kinesis Data Analytics with Flink) processes events continuously with sub-minute latency. Full daily rewrites scale with total data; weekly reloads still reprocess; no dedup compounds the waste.
Athena — provides serverless SQL directly on S3, paying per byte scanned — perfect for low-volume ad-hoc analysis.
Common trap — amazon Managed Streaming for Kafka + Flink (or Kinesis Data Analytics).
Skipping the key question — which service runs serverless Spark with auto-scaling.
Skipping the key question — which service gives you a managed big-data cluster with many frameworks.

Lambda — Lambda scales from zero to 10k concurrent executions for short event-driven transforms with per-millisecond billing. Always-on EC2 idles at zero; EMR is for cluster analytics, not 200ms functions; bare metal is the opposite of elastic.

Data lineage — the Glue Data Catalog with lineage tracking records how data flows and transforms from source to report — the auditable answer. Data mesh distributes ownership to domain teams who publish data products with contracts/SLAs, scaling ownership with the organiz…

Data — Data quality rules (e.g., Glue Data Quality / Deequ checks) in the pipeline validate schema, completeness, and ranges, quarantining failures before they corrupt downstream.
Common trap — data mesh principles: domain ownership + data products with contracts.
Common trap — lake Formation fine-grained permissions (table/column/row level).
Common trap — S3 Lifecycle policies aligned to retention requirements.
Common trap — everyone gets full access.

S3 Lifecycle — S3 Lifecycle policies enforce per-dataset retention and archival automatically at 3 TB/day scale. Keeping everything forever wastes money and may violate minimization; manual reviews don't scale; no policy is non-compliance.

Step Functions — Step Functions orchestrates serverless workflows with visual execution graphs, per-state retries/catches, and integrations to Lambda, Glue, and more. Pipeline-native monitoring (Airflow SLAs, Step Functions/CloudWatch alarms on task duration) watches every…
Event-driven — Event-driven triggers (S3 Event Notifications, EventBridge) start pipelines on arrival with low latency, and idempotent tasks make duplicate events safe.

Failure handling — manual Lambda chaining reinvents error handling; one giant Lambda couples everything; bash on EC2 is fragile. Blind infinite retries are the current failure; ignoring/deleting loses data.
Common trap — event-driven triggers (S3 events, EventBridge) + idempotent tasks.
Common trap — separate dev/staging/prod with promotion of tested artifacts.
Common trap — lambda alone for 50-step DAGs.
Common trap — one pipeline for dev and prod.

items: QuickSight — row-level (and column-level) security in QuickSight and Lake Formation filters data by viewer identity — enforced, not advisory. QuickSight provides managed BI with SPICE in-memory engine, integrating natively with AWS data sources and scaling to hundreds o…
BI — BI: one-off queries repeat the waste; bigger warehouses just scan faster at higher cost; BI-only caching is fragile. Custom builds reintroduce ops; email chains and screenshots aren't BI.
ML for analysts — redshift ML and SageMaker Canvas let analysts build and use models with SQL or no-code interfaces against warehouse data in place.
Open table formats (Apache Hudi, Iceberg — supported by Athena, EMR, Glue) bring upserts, deletes, and time travel to S3 data lakes.
Materialized — Materialized views or scheduled aggregation tables precompute the repeated aggregations once, so dashboards read megabytes instead of terabytes.
Common trap — materialized views / scheduled aggregations.
Common trap — cost allocation tags + query-level cost attribution (e.g., Athena workgroups, Redshift concurrency scaling) + lifecycle policies.
